Picture a dying campfire. The flames are shrinking, the logs are barely glowing. You grab a stick, poke the embers, rearrange the wood, and toss in more fuel. The fire roars back to life, burning hotter and stronger than before. That whole act — feeding a fire, tending to it, making it burn harder — is what "stoke" literally means.

This single image is the key to understanding everything this word does.
Meaning 1: The literal sense — tending a fire

To stoke a fire, a furnace, or a boiler means to add fuel to it and tend to it so it keeps burning well.

  • She stoked the fireplace before the guests arrived.
  • Workers stoked the furnace with coal all through the night.

The person whose job it was to do this (especially on a ship or in a factory) was called a stoker.

This is the original, physical meaning. Everything else the word does grows out of this image.
Meaning 2 (most common): Making a feeling or situation grow stronger

This is where "stoke" earns most of its power in modern English. Just as you stoke a fire by feeding it fuel, you can stoke an emotion, a conflict, or a tension — meaning you do something that makes it grow bigger, hotter, and harder to control.

The key idea: something already exists, and you are feeding it so it intensifies.

  • The politician's speech stoked fear among voters. (The fear was already there; the speech made it much stronger.)
  • The rumours stoked tensions between the two communities.
  • His silence only stoked people's curiosity.
  • The article stoked outrage across the country.

Notice what kind of things typically get stoked: fear, anger, outrage, tension, conflict, controversy, curiosity, passion. These are all things that, like fire, have the capacity to grow and spread if fed.

Also notice: when someone or something "stokes" a feeling, there is usually an agent — a person, a speech, an event — doing the stoking, whether deliberately or not. And the result is powerful, often difficult to contain. Just like a real fire.

A very natural phrasing you'll encounter: to stoke the flames of something — for example, "His comments stoked the flames of controversy." This is a direct echo of the literal meaning.
Meaning 3: Generating or building up something positive

"Stoke" doesn't only apply to negative or dangerous things. It can also mean to build up or generate something desirable — especially appetite, enthusiasm, or motivation.

  • The long hike stoked our appetites. (It built up our hunger powerfully.)
  • The trailer stoked excitement for the new film. (It generated and fuelled enthusiasm.)
  • Her speech stoked the team's passion before the match.

Here the word means: to produce and intensify something through action. You're still feeding something so it grows stronger — just in a good direction this time.

In casual, everyday speech — especially in American English — "stoke" is used to mean to fill someone with excitement or enthusiasm.

  • That news really stoked me. (It made me very excited.)

However, in this sense you'll almost always encounter it as the adjective stoked (the past participle used as a describing word), rather than as an active verb:

  • I am so stoked about the concert! → I am extremely excited and thrilled.
  • She was completely stoked when she got the job.
  • We're all stoked for the trip.

"Stoked" in this sense means: deeply enthusiastic, pumped up, thrilled. It's warm, energetic, and positive. The tone is always informal — this is something you'd say to friends or in casual writing, not in a formal essay or professional setting. It originated in surf and skate culture in California and has spread widely through everyday American speech.

Understanding a word fully means knowing how it sits among its neighbours.

Stoke vs. ignite: To ignite something is to start it from nothing — to spark it into existence. To stoke something means it was already there; you are feeding it and making it stronger. You ignite a fire, then stoke it.

Stoke vs. fuel (verb): These are very close in the figurative sense — "fuel the debate" and "stoke the debate" mean nearly the same thing. But "stoke" is more vivid and physical; it paints a picture of someone actively tending something. "Fuel" is slightly more neutral.

Stoke vs. fan (as in "fan the flames"): Both suggest making something grow. "Fan" often implies something barely alive being revived. "Stoke" implies more deliberate, sustained feeding.

Stoke vs. intensify: "Intensify" is neutral and clinical. "Stoke" is vivid and implies an active agent doing something that makes things hotter and harder to control.
Summary — the one idea behind all four meanings

Whether literal or figurative, positive or negative, formal or casual — "stoke" always comes back to the same core idea:

To feed something that has the capacity to burn, and make it burn stronger.

You stoke a fire with wood. You stoke fear with alarming words. You stoke appetite with a long walk. And when someone is stoked, they are burning with excitement.

Once you see that central flame, every use of the word makes perfect sense.
